Literal Interpretation

The Divine Appearance and Name "El Shaddai"

Genesis 17 opens with a theophany: "And after he began to be ninety and nine years old, the Lord appeared to him: and said unto him: I am the Almighty God: walk before me, and be perfect" (Gen 17:1). This is the first occurrence in Scripture of the divine name "El Shaddai" (God Almighty), marking a significant revelation of God's character. The Hebrew term Shaddai has been variously interpreted as deriving from shadû ("mountain"), suggesting strength and immovability, or from shad ("breast"), suggesting nourishing sufficiency. The Septuagint renders it as "παντοκράτωρ" (Pantokrator, "Almighty"), and this is followed by the Vulgate's "Omnipotens."

The timing is significant: Abram is ninety-nine years old, and Sarai is eighty-nine and well beyond natural fertility. When both are "as good as dead" regarding procreation, God reveals Himself as El Shaddai—the God who does what is humanly impossible. The command to "walk before me and be perfect" (tamim) calls for wholehearted devotion and integrity, not sinless perfection.

The Change of Name: Abram to Abraham

"Neither shall thy name be called any more Abram: but thou shalt be called Abraham: because I have made thee a father of many nations" (Gen 17:5). In Hebrew, "Abram" means "exalted father," while "Abraham" is understood to mean "father of a multitude" or "father of many nations." The addition of the letter he (ה) to Abram's name is traditionally seen as significant—this letter appears twice in the divine name YHWH, suggesting that something of God's own identity is now imparted to Abraham.

St. Jerome, in his Liber interpretationis hebraicorum nominum (Book of Interpretation of Hebrew Names), systematically catalogued the meanings of biblical names. Jerome, the only Church Father with genuine command of Hebrew, studied with Jewish teachers in Bethlehem and attained such proficiency that his transcriptions remain valuable for understanding ancient Hebrew pronunciation.

Sarai to Sarah

Similarly, "Sarai thy wife thou shalt not call Sarai, but Sara" (Gen 17:15). Both names mean "princess," but the change from the archaic form to the standard Hebrew form signifies her elevation to mother of nations and kings. Where Sarai was "my princess" (a more limited term), Sarah becomes simply "princess"—a queen mother of universal significance.

The Covenant of Circumcision

"This is my covenant which you shall observe, between me and you, and thy seed after thee: All the male kind of you shall be circumcised" (Gen 17:10). Circumcision is established as the sign (oth) of the covenant. Unlike the covenant with Noah (Gen 9), which was one-sided and unconditional, this covenant requires something of man—a physical mark of covenant membership.

The specification of the eighth day (Gen 17:12) is noteworthy both medically and theologically. Modern medicine recognizes that vitamin K and prothrombin levels, essential for blood clotting, reach their peak on the eighth day of life. Theologically, the number eight transcends the seven days of creation, pointing toward new creation and resurrection.

St. Augustine, in his City of God, Book XVI, addresses this passage extensively. He notes that at the time when Abraham believed and his faith was counted to him for righteousness (Gen 15:6), Abraham had not yet been circumcised. This chronological detail is crucial: faith preceded circumcision, demonstrating that righteousness comes through faith rather than through the sign that sealed it.

The Severity of the Covenant

"The male, whose flesh of his foreskin shall not be circumcised, that soul shall be cut off from his people: because he hath broken my covenant" (Gen 17:14). The penalty for neglecting circumcision is being "cut off" (karath)—the same verb used for "cutting" a covenant. The wordplay is intentional: the one who refuses to be cut in covenant will be cut off from the covenant people. Augustine interprets this commandment as pointing toward the necessity of formal entry into God's people—a principle fulfilled in Christian baptism.

The Promise Concerning Ishmael and Isaac

When Abraham laughs at the promise of a son through Sarah and proposes that Ishmael might be the heir (Gen 17:17-18), God distinguishes between the two sons. Ishmael will be blessed and become a great nation, but the covenant will be established specifically with Isaac, who will be born the following year. The name "Isaac" (Yitzchak) means "he laughs," memorializing both Abraham's laughter and the joy that would attend his miraculous birth.

Abraham's Immediate Obedience

The chapter concludes with Abraham's prompt obedience: "And Abraham took Ismael his son, and all that were born in his house: and all whom he had bought, every male among the men of his house: and he circumcised the flesh of their foreskin forthwith the very same day, as God had commanded him" (Gen 17:23). Abraham was ninety-nine years old and Ishmael was thirteen when they were circumcised "on that very day"—the same phrase used of Noah entering the ark (Gen 7:13), emphasizing decisive obedience without delay.
allegorical:
Allegorical Interpretation

Circumcision as Type of Baptism

The Church Fathers unanimously interpreted circumcision as a type prefiguring Christian baptism. St. John Chrysostom states explicitly:

"Circumcision is no longer performed with a knife, Paul says, but in Christ himself; for no human hand circumcises... but the Spirit. The Spirit circumcises the whole man, not simply a part.... When and where? In baptism."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Colossians 6 (c. 395 A.D.)

St. Cyril of Alexandria develops this typology further:

"On the eighth day Christ arose from the dead, and gave us the spiritual circumcision. For He commanded the holy Apostles: 'Having gone, make ye disciples of all nations, baptizing them into the Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.' The spiritual circumcision takes place chiefly in the season of holy baptism, when also Christ makes us partakers of the Holy Ghost."

St. Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke

Cyril also uses Joshua as a type:

"And of this again, that Jesus of old, who was captain after Moses, was a type. For he first of all led the children of Israel across the Jordan: and then having halted them, immediately circumcised them with knives of stone. So when we have crossed the Jordan, Christ circumcises us with the power of the Holy Ghost, not purifying the flesh, but rather cutting off the defilement that is in our souls."

St. Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke

The connection between circumcision and baptism is further affirmed by Cyril:

"Circumcision prefigured in itself the grace and efficacy of Divine baptism; for as in old time he that was circumcised, was reckoned among the people of God by that seal, so also he that is baptized, having formed in himself Christ the seal, is enrolled into God's adopted family."

St. Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke

The Eighth Day and the Resurrection

St. Augustine draws a profound connection between the eighth day of circumcision and the resurrection of Christ:

"This is the octave day of your new birth. Today is fulfilled in you the sign of faith that was prefigured in the Old Testament by the circumcision of the flesh on the eighth day after birth. When the Lord rose from the dead, he put off the mortality of the flesh; his risen body was still the same body, but it was no longer subject to death. By his resurrection he consecrated Sunday, or the Lord's day. Though the third after his passion, this day is the eighth after the Sabbath, and thus also the first day of the week."

St. Augustine, Sermo 8 in octava Paschae (Easter Octave Sermon)

Augustine further explains in his letters:

"The sacramental import of the eighth number, as signifying the resurrection, was by no means concealed from the holy men of old who were filled with the spirit of prophecy... infants were circumcised on the eighth day."

St. Augustine, Letter 55

The Name Change as New Creation

The change from Abram to Abraham prefigures the new identity given in baptism. Just as Abraham received a new name signifying his new calling as father of many nations, so the Christian receives a new identity in Christ. St. Justin Martyr in his Dialogue with Trypho explains:

"We who have approached God through Him have received not carnal, but spiritual circumcision, which Enoch and those like him observed. And we have received it through baptism."

St. Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho (c. 155-160 A.D.)

Abraham as Type of Christ

St. Irenaeus, in his Against Heresies, establishes the typological connection between Abraham and Christ:

"Abraham did also receive the covenant of circumcision, after that justification by faith which had pertained to him, when he was yet in uncircumcision, so that in him both covenants might be prefigured, that he might be the father of all who follow the Word of God."

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book IV, Chapter 25

Irenaeus further explains that circumcision was given as a recognizable sign for the chosen people:

"God gave circumcision, not as the completer of righteousness, but as a sign, that the race of Abraham might continue recognisable.... Abraham himself, without circumcision and without observance of Sabbaths, believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness."

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book IV, Chapter 16

The Two Covenants Prefigured

Irenaeus sees in Abraham the prefiguration of both Old and New Covenants:

"Both covenants were prefigured in Abraham.... He gathered into the one faith of Abraham those who, from either covenant, are eligible for God's building. But this faith which is in uncircumcision, as connecting the end with the beginning, has been made both the first and the last. For, as I have shown, it existed in Abraham antecedently to circumcision."

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book IV, Chapter 25

Circumcision and the Passion

St. Augustine in Contra Faustum explains how circumcision pointed to Christ's death:

"Because we are justified by faith in Christ's resurrection, the apostle says, 'He died for our offenses, and rose again for our justification.' And because this resurrection by faith in which we are justified was prefigured by the circumcision of the eighth day, the apostle says of Abraham, with whom the observance began, 'He received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith.' Circumcision, then, is one of the prophecies of Christ, written by Moses, of whom Christ said, 'He wrote of me.'"

St. Augustine, Contra Faustum, Book XVI

Spiritual Circumcision Through Christ's Words

St. Justin Martyr interprets the "knives of stone" used by Joshua as a type of Christ's teaching:

"Joshua circumcised the people a second time with knives of stone, which was a sign of this circumcision with which Jesus Christ Himself has circumcised us from the idols made of stone and of other materials. The 'knives of stone' mean Christ's words, by means of which so many who were in error have been circumcised from uncircumcision with the circumcision of the heart."

St. Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho
moral:
Moral (Tropological) Interpretation

Walking Before God in Integrity

The divine command to Abraham, "Walk before me, and be perfect" (Gen 17:1), establishes the fundamental pattern of the moral life. To "walk before God" means to live consciously in His presence, ordering all one's actions as if under the divine gaze. The Hebrew tamim ("perfect" or "blameless") does not demand sinless perfection but wholehearted integrity—a life undivided in its devotion to God.

The Circumcision of the Heart

The physical rite of circumcision was always understood to point toward an interior reality. St. Basil the Great, in his Sermon on Holy Baptism, exhorts:

"The Jew does not delay circumcision, being mindful of the threat, that 'every soul that is not circumcised on the eighth day, shall be destroyed out of her people:' and you delay the circumcision—not that which is made by hands, in the stripping of the flesh, but that which is accomplished in baptism. And in that ceremony pain was endured, and an ulcer was caused: but in this the soul is refreshed with heavenly dew, and the ulcers of the heart are healed."

St. Basil the Great, Sermon 13 on Holy Baptism

The moral teaching is clear:

"The circumcision of the flesh was very painful, but beneficial. Similarly, the circumcision of the heart, that is, the cutting off evil inclinations, is sorrowful, but beneficial."

Traditional patristic teaching on the Feast of the Circumcision

We are called to cut away fleshly passions that enslave us and prevent spiritual life, dedicating ourselves totally to God in body and soul.

Cutting Off Sin and Passion

St. Justin Martyr applies the image of circumcision to the moral life:

"And our hearts are thus circumcised from evil, so that we are happy to die for the name of the good Rock, which causes living water to burst forth for the hearts of those who by Him have loved the Father of all."

St. Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho

Justin further exhorts his Jewish interlocutor (and all readers) to interior transformation:

"Be circumcised from hard-heartedness: not that circumcision which you have from the tenets that are put into you; for that was given for a sign, and not for a work of righteousness, as the Scriptures compel you to admit."

St. Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho

Faith Before Works

St. Irenaeus emphasizes that Abraham's moral standing before God was established through faith, not through external observance:

"Man was not justified by these things, but that they were given as a sign to the people.... Abraham himself, without circumcision and without observance of Sabbaths, believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness. Lot was saved without circumcision, Noah pleased God while uncircumcised, and Enoch pleased God without circumcision. Moreover, all the rest of the multitude of those righteous men who lived before Abraham, and of those patriarchs who preceded Moses, were justified independently of the things above mentioned, and without the law of Moses."

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book IV, Chapter 16

The moral lesson is that external religious observance, however important, cannot substitute for interior faith and righteousness. The sign must correspond to the reality it signifies.

Immediate Obedience

Abraham's response to God's command is a model of prompt obedience. When God commanded circumcision, Abraham did not delay or seek excuses: he circumcised himself and his entire household "on that very day" (Gen 17:23, 26). This immediate response, despite the pain involved for a ninety-nine-year-old man, demonstrates the proper disposition of faith: trust that acts without hesitation.

The moral application extends to all divine commands. When God speaks—through Scripture, through the Church, through conscience—the faithful response is not negotiation or delay but willing obedience. Abraham's example shames our tendency to rationalize delay or partial compliance.

The Cost of Covenant

Circumcision was painful, especially for adults. Abraham, Ishmael, and all the men of the household endured this pain as the cost of covenant membership. The moral lesson is that genuine relationship with God requires sacrifice. As Tertullian later observed, responding to those who thought faith alone was sufficient without the sacramental sign:

"In days gone by, there was salvation by means of bare faith, before the passion and resurrection of the Lord. But now that faith has been enlarged, there has been an amplification added to the sacrament, viz., the sealing act of baptism."

Tertullian, On Baptism

Belonging to God's People

The severe penalty for neglecting circumcision—being "cut off" from the people—teaches the seriousness of covenant membership. One cannot claim the benefits of God's promises while refusing the obligations they entail. In Christian terms, baptism is not optional for those who would follow Christ; it is the appointed means of entry into His covenant people.

Consecration of the Whole Person

Circumcision marked the organ of generation, consecrating human fertility to God's purposes. The moral application extends to the consecration of all human powers and capacities to divine service. Nothing in human nature is exempt from God's claim; every faculty must be brought under the lordship of Christ.
anagogical:
Anagogical Interpretation

The Eighth Day and Eternal Life

The specification that circumcision occur on the eighth day carries profound eschatological significance. The number eight transcends the seven days of creation, pointing toward the "eighth day" that has no evening—the eternal Sabbath rest of heaven. St. Augustine expounds this connection:

"By his resurrection he consecrated Sunday, or the Lord's day. Though the third after his passion, this day is the eighth after the Sabbath, and thus also the first day of the week."

St. Augustine, Easter Octave Sermon

Augustine further declares:

"Such is the power of this sacrament: it is a sacrament of new life which begins here and now with the forgiveness of all past sins, and will be brought to completion in the resurrection of the dead."

St. Augustine, On Baptism, Against the Donatists

The eighth day circumcision thus points toward the resurrection of the body and the life of the world to come. What begins in baptismal regeneration will be completed in the general resurrection, when the mortal puts on immortality.

The Everlasting Covenant

"And I will establish my covenant between me and thee, and between thy seed after thee in their generations, by a perpetual covenant" (Gen 17:7). The covenant is described as olam—everlasting, perpetual, eternal. This "everlasting covenant" finds its ultimate fulfillment not in any temporal arrangement but in the eternal kingdom of God.

St. Irenaeus affirms the eternal nature of God's covenant promises:

"One and the same householder produced both covenants, the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who spake with both Abraham and Moses."

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book IV

The New Covenant, established in Christ's blood, is eternal because its Mediator is both God and man. Unlike temporal covenants that can be broken, the covenant sealed by divine blood endures forever.

Father of Many Nations

The promise that Abraham would be "father of many nations" extends beyond earthly progeny to the communion of saints. St. Augustine distinguishes the twofold nature of the promise:

"Two things are promised to Abraham, the one, that his seed should possess the land of Canaan... but the other far more excellent, not about the carnal but the spiritual seed, through which he is the father, not of the one Israelite nation, but of all nations who follow the footprints of his faith."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI

The "many nations" who call Abraham father include the innumerable multitude from every tribe and tongue who will stand before the throne of God. The earthly Israel was a sign pointing toward the heavenly assembly; the promised inheritance was a shadow of the eternal homeland.

The New Name in Glory

The change of name from Abram to Abraham prefigures the eschatological promise: "To him that overcometh, I will give... a white counter, and in the counter, a new name written, which no man knoweth, but he that receiveth it" (Rev 2:17). In heaven, each of the blessed will receive a new name from God, expressing their unique identity in the divine plan and their eternal relationship with the Creator.

As Abraham's new name expressed his calling as father of nations, so the new names given to the saints will express their completed identity in Christ—who they were created to be, fully realized in glory.

The Heavenly Jerusalem

God's promise to Abraham, "I will give to thee, and to thy seed, the land of thy sojournment, all the land of Chanaan for a perpetual possession" (Gen 17:8), finds its ultimate fulfillment not in earthly Canaan but in the heavenly Jerusalem. The Letter to the Hebrews affirms that Abraham "looked for a city which hath foundations; whose builder and maker is God" (Heb 11:10).

The earthly promised land, flowing with milk and honey, was but a type of that eternal country where God dwells with His people, where there is no more death or mourning or pain, where the river of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb.

The Beatific Vision

The divine appearance to Abraham—"the Lord appeared to him" (Gen 17:1)—anticipates the beatific vision that constitutes the essence of heavenly blessedness. What Abraham saw partially and fleetingly, the blessed will see fully and eternally. "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face" (1 Cor 13:12).

The progressive revelation of God's name—from Elohim to El Shaddai to YHWH to the full revelation in Christ—points toward the final unveiling when we shall know God as we are known. The names of God disclosed in Scripture are but approaches to the ineffable reality that will be our eternal contemplation.

The Resurrection of the Body

Augustine interprets circumcision in terms of the resurrection:

"Circumcision as a symbol of the resurrection—as a removal of the mortality of the flesh."

Patristic interpretation following St. Augustine

The cutting away of flesh in circumcision signified the putting off of corruption and mortality. In the resurrection, believers will be "clothed with immortality" (1 Cor 15:53), their bodies transformed to be like Christ's glorious body. The mark of circumcision, borne in mortal flesh, pointed toward this ultimate transformation when the perishable puts on the imperishable.

Eternal Fruitfulness

The promise of descendants "as the stars of heaven" and "as the sand of the sea" (cf. Gen 22:17) extends into eternity. The spiritual offspring of Abraham—all who share his faith—will shine in the kingdom of heaven: "Then shall the just shine as the sun, in the kingdom of their Father" (Mt 13:43). The fruitfulness promised to Abraham finds its ultimate expression in the communion of saints, an ever-growing multitude praising God forever.
